# Canonical Encoding and Typed Hashing

Every guarantee in Part III rests on hashing and signing bytes. A signature
chain link is a signed byte string; a Merkle leaf is the hash of a byte
string; a Merkle root is a signed byte string that contains the hashes of
other byte strings. None of that works unless two parties who hold the same
logical object produce the same bytes for it. This chapter is about how FOKS
makes that true, and about the second, related problem: making sure that a
signature over one kind of object can never be mistaken for a signature over
another.

## The problem: signatures cover bytes, not meanings

A digital signature scheme signs a sequence of bytes. Application code, on
the other hand, deals in structures: a link with a sequence number, a
previous-hash field, a list of key changes. Between the two sits a
serialization format, and most serialization formats allow one structure to
be written in several ways. JSON does not fix the order of object keys or the
spelling of numbers. Protocol Buffers allow unknown fields and multiple
encodings of the same integer. Even a compact binary format like MessagePack
lets the integer 5 be written as one byte or as two, three, five, or nine.

If a verifier re-serializes a structure and hashes the result, it must get the
same bytes the signer hashed, or the signature fails for no good reason. Worse,
if two different structures can serialize to the same bytes, a signature over
one is a valid signature over the other. The standard remedy is a *canonical
encoding*: a rule under which every value has exactly one byte representation
and every byte string decodes to at most one value. XML Canonicalization and
ASN.1's Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) are the well-known examples; FOKS
uses a canonical subset of MessagePack.

FOKS has a second reason to care. The Rust implementation must interoperate
with the reference Go implementation (go-foks v0.1.9). A link signed by a Go
client must verify in Rust and land at the same Merkle leaf; a root signed by
a Rust server must verify in Go. "Same bytes" therefore means byte-for-byte
identical output across two independent code bases that never exchange a
schema at runtime.

## MessagePack in one page

MessagePack is a binary serialization format in which every value begins with
a one-byte *marker* that identifies its type and, for small values, carries
the value itself. Small integers, short strings, short arrays, and small maps
each fit in a single marker byte; larger values use a marker followed by a
length or the value in big-endian form.

| Marker bytes    | Meaning                                    |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `0x00`–`0x7f`   | positive fixint (the value is the marker)  |
| `0x80`–`0x8f`   | fixmap, 0–15 entries                       |
| `0x90`–`0x9f`   | fixarray, 0–15 elements                    |
| `0xa0`–`0xbf`   | fixstr, 0–31 bytes                         |
| `0xc0`          | nil                                        |
| `0xc2`, `0xc3`  | false, true                                |
| `0xc4`–`0xc6`   | bin8, bin16, bin32                         |
| `0xc7`–`0xc9`, `0xd4`–`0xd8` | extension types                |
| `0xca`, `0xcb`  | float32, float64                           |
| `0xcc`–`0xcf`   | uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64              |
| `0xd0`–`0xd3`   | int8, int16, int32, int64                  |
| `0xd9`–`0xdb`   | str8, str16, str32                         |
| `0xdc`, `0xdd`  | array16, array32                           |
| `0xde`, `0xdf`  | map16, map32                               |
| `0xe0`–`0xff`   | negative fixint, −32 to −1                 |

The format is compact and simple to parse, but it is not canonical. The
integer 200 can be a `uint8`, a `uint16`, a `uint32`, or a `uint64`. A
three-element array can be a fixarray or an `array16`. A map's entries can
appear in any order. Floats have two widths. Extension types let applications
define new markers. A canonical profile must remove every one of these
choices.

## Snowpack: a canonical subset

Snowpack is the name go-foks gives to its MessagePack profile, and
`foks-snowpack` is the Rust crate that implements it. The crate's own
description is that it is "not a general-purpose MessagePack codec." Its data
model has only eight kinds of value:

| Value kind   | Wire form                                                   |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Null`       | `0xc0`                                                      |
| `Bool`       | `0xc2` or `0xc3`                                            |
| `Unsigned`   | shortest of fixint, uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64           |
| `Negative`   | shortest of negative fixint, int8, int16, int32, int64      |
| `Binary`     | bin8, bin16, or bin32 with the smallest header that fits    |
| `Text`       | fixstr, str8, str16, or str32 with the smallest header      |
| `Array`      | fixarray, array16, or array32; never empty                  |
| `Variant`    | fixmap with zero entries, or one entry keyed by a fixstr    |

Two structural conventions turn Go structs into these values.

**Structs are positional arrays.** A struct with fields `a`, `b`, `c` is
encoded as a three-element array in declaration order. Field names never
appear on the wire, so there is no key-ordering question and no way to omit or
duplicate a field. (This is go-codec's `toarray` option, which go-foks uses
for every protocol type.)

**Tagged unions are one-entry maps.** A union with no arm set is the empty
fixmap `0x80`. A union with an arm set is the one-entry fixmap `0x81` whose
key is a short string tag of at most 31 bytes and whose value is the arm's
payload. These are the only maps Snowpack permits. Key ordering therefore
never arises inside a canonical object; where FOKS's RPC envelope carries
ordinary named-field maps, the keys appear in sorted order, and that belongs
to [Chapter 17](17-wire.qmd).

On top of those conventions, the encoder and decoder enforce minimality:

- Unsigned integers use the shortest marker: `0`–`127` as a fixint, then
  uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64. The decoder rejects, for example, a `uint8`
  marker followed by a byte of `0x7f` or less.
- Negative integers likewise, and the `Negative` kind refuses to hold zero
  or a positive number, so `+5` has exactly one form and so does `−5`.
- Binary and text lengths use the smallest header; a `bin16` with a length
  under 256 is rejected.
- Arrays are never empty. An empty list is represented as `Null` at the
  schema level. The decoder treats the empty fixarray `0x90` as an error.
- Floats, extension types, the reserved marker `0xc1`, `map16`, `map32`, and
  fixmaps with two or more entries are all errors.
- Nothing may follow the value: trailing bytes are an error.
- Nesting depth is capped at 64 and the total number of decoded values at
  1,000,000, and an array header claiming more elements than there are bytes
  remaining is rejected before any allocation.

The last group is defensive rather than canonical. Snowpack frames arrive
from the network, and a decoder that allocated whatever a header asked for
would be an easy target.

## One encoding per value, and how that is tested

The property Snowpack promises is that `decode(encode(v)) = v` for every
canonical value `v`, and `encode(decode(b)) = b` for every byte string `b` the
decoder accepts. Together these say the mapping between values and byte
strings is a bijection on the accepted set: one encoding per value, one value
per encoding.

`foks-snowpack` tests this with QuickCheck-style property tests. A generator
builds random values from all eight kinds, choosing top-level array lengths
from the boundary set 1, 2, 7, 15, 16, 17, 31, 32, and 33 so that the
fixarray, array16, and array32 transitions are exercised. Two thousand random
values are encoded, decoded, and compared, and every shrink of a failing case
must itself remain canonical. Alongside the property tests, a directory of
byte fixtures written by the Go implementation is round-tripped byte-exactly;
each fixture was accepted by Go's own canonical checker before it was written,
so the fixtures are evidence about Go, not a Rust reimplementation of Go.

## Signing the delivered bytes

Canonical encoding solves the problem of two encoders disagreeing. A second
technique removes the need for a verifier to re-encode at all. Wherever a
signed object is embedded in a larger one, the inner object's exact encoding
is carried as an opaque `Binary` value:

- A `SignedBlob` is the two-element array `[Binary(inner), signature]`. The
  Merkle root and the host's public zone travel this way.
- A chain link's outer form is `[1, {"1": [Binary(inner), [signatures]]}]`,
  and the Rust `UserLink` type keeps `inner` verbatim, with the comment that
  "both stacked signatures and the Merkle leaf commit to these bytes."

The verifier checks the signature over the bytes it was given, then decodes
those bytes to learn what they say. It never has to reproduce them. This is
what makes forward compatibility workable: the decoder for a Merkle root
accepts *at least* five fields, keeps any trailing fields it does not
understand, and re-encodes them unchanged, so a root minted by a newer server
still hashes and verifies correctly on an older client.

The leading `1` and the `"1"` tag in the outer form both carry a version
number. That redundancy is how go-foks's versioned unions serialize, and
Snowpack preserves it because changing it would change the bytes.

## Typed hashing

The second problem in this chapter is *domain separation*. Suppose a Merkle
root and some other protocol object happened to encode to the same bytes. A
signature made over one would then be a valid signature over the other, and a
verifier could be handed the wrong object with a genuine signature. Canonical
encoding does not prevent this; it only guarantees that each object has one
encoding, not that different kinds of object have different encodings.

FOKS's answer is to assign every object kind a 64-bit *type ID* and to prepend
it, as eight big-endian bytes, to the encoded object before hashing or
signing. The hash function throughout is SHA-512/256, the FIPS 180-4 variant
of SHA-512 that uses a distinct initial value and truncates to 256 bits:

$$
\mathrm{prefixed\_hash}(t, m) = \mathrm{SHA\text{-}512/256}(\mathrm{BE64}(t) \,\|\, m)
$$

Signatures are computed over the same prefixed message, and keyed
commitments use HMAC-SHA-512/256 with the same layout: the type ID, then the
canonical bytes. A selection of the constants used in Part III:

| Constant                          | Value                  | Used for                          |
|-----------------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| `LINK_OUTER_TYPE_ID`              | `0xed4cc0f7081732b6`   | hash of a user or team link       |
| `LINK_OUTER_V1_TYPE_ID`           | `0xc2745284af617745`   | signatures on a user or team link |
| `HOSTCHAIN_LINK_OUTER_TYPE_ID`    | `0x8d87ac224920355c`   | hash of a hostchain link          |
| `MERKLE_NODE_TYPE_ID`             | `0xe941750dc5b96783`   | hash of a tree node               |
| `MERKLE_ROOT_TYPE_ID`             | `0xa88fc49b6df3a111`   | hash of a Merkle root             |
| `MERKLE_ROOT_BLOB_TYPE_ID`        | `0xa22f0c0921d4e651`   | signature on a Merkle root        |
| `MERKLE_BACK_POINTERS_TYPE_ID`    | `0x8c7c4b855fba9000`   | hash of an epoch's back pointers  |
| `MERKLE_TREE_RF_INPUT_TYPE_ID`    | `0xb0e268f388acc97a`   | derivation of a tree key          |
| `TREE_LOCATION_TYPE_ID`           | `0xaeffd88b6cd267d9`   | commitment to a tree location     |
| `CHAIN_LOCATION_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID` | `0xe516acf96cf56e58` | subchain start location           |
| `NAME_COMMITMENT_TYPE_ID`         | `0xe37b1fcfba972353`   | username commitment               |

The values are fixed by the Go implementation and copied into
`foks-proto`; they look random because they are. Note that a link has two
type IDs, one for its hash and one for the signatures over it, and a root
likewise. Hashing an object and signing it are different operations on
different byte strings, and the type IDs keep them apart. The same technique
extends beyond hashing: [Chapter 4](04-hybrid-encryption.qmd) shows the
type ID placed in the first eight bytes of an authenticated-encryption nonce
so that a ciphertext produced for one purpose cannot be opened under another.

Domain separation by prefix is a standard construction. NIST SP 800-185
formalizes it for the SHA-3 family (cSHAKE's customization string), and most
modern protocols do something equivalent with a label. The FOKS variant is
unusual only in using a 64-bit integer rather than a human-readable string.

## `validate` versus `validate_signable`

There is one place where "shortest marker" and "what Go's canonical checker
accepts" disagree, and it affects every signature in the system. A fixarray
holds at most 15 elements, so an array of 16 to 31 elements has no shorter
form than `array16`. The Rust encoder emits `array16` for those lengths, and
they are legitimately needed: the signup RPC argument has 16 fields. But
go-foks's canonicality check for signed and hashed objects rejects *every*
`array16` whose length is 31 or less, including those with no shorter form.

`foks-snowpack` therefore offers two validation modes:

| Function             | `array16` of length 16–31 | Used by                          |
|----------------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------|
| `validate`           | accepted                  | the RPC codec                    |
| `validate_signable`  | rejected                  | every hash, signature, and HMAC  |

Every primitive in `foks-crypto` that hashes or signs a protocol object calls
`validate_signable` first: `prefixed_hash_signable`, `sign_ed25519_typed`,
`sign_ed25519_blob` (which validates both the inner bytes and the binary
wrapper the signature covers, since a wrapper around arbitrary bytes is
itself a valid `Binary` value), and their verification counterparts. The rule this enforces is simple to
state: refuse to sign anything the reference implementation would refuse to
verify. A Rust client cannot produce a link that a Go server rejects, and a
Rust server cannot mint a root that a Go client rejects.

The rule has a consequence that is easy to miss. An object with 16 to 31
elements in any array cannot be signed or hashed at all, by either
implementation. [Chapter 12](12-epochs.qmd) shows where that bites: the
epoch whose back-pointer list first reaches 16 entries cannot be published.

## Trade-offs

A canonical subset gives up flexibility. There are no floats, so anything
fractional (team index ranges, for instance) is encoded as a rational with an
explicit base and exponent. There are no general maps, so every schema change
that adds a field must append it at the end of a positional array. Empty lists
cost a special case in every decoder. In exchange, hashing serialized bytes is
safe, there is no separate canonicalization step that could drift between
implementations, and the entire canonical surface is small enough to test
exhaustively at the marker level.

Wrapping inner encodings as opaque binaries costs a few bytes per level of
nesting and means a verifier holds two copies of a link's content, one as
bytes and one decoded. It buys independence from re-serialization, which is
the single most common source of cross-implementation signature failures.

Typed hashing costs eight bytes per hash input and a registry of constants
that must never collide. It removes an entire class of confusion attacks, and
the registry doubles as documentation of every object the protocol
authenticates.

## Where to look

- `foks-snowpack`: the `Value` model, `encode`, `decode`, `validate`, and
  `validate_signable`; property tests and Go fixtures under `tests/`.
- `foks-proto`: the type ID constants in the crate root; `codec` for the
  positional accessors; `SignedBlob`, `HostchainLink`, `MerkleRoot`, and
  `UserLink` for the opaque-binary wrapping.
- `foks-crypto`: `prefixed_hash`, `prefixed_hash_signable`,
  `sign_ed25519_typed`, `sign_ed25519_blob`, and `commitment`.
- `tools/foks-v019-oracle`: the Go program that writes the fixtures after
  Go's own canonical checker accepts them.
